{'included_studies_json': '[{"study_index": 1, "title": "Promoting HIV testing and condom use among Filipina
commercial sex workers: findings from a quasi‐experimental intervention study", "abstract": "This study examines the
effects of a multi-level social action-based theory (SABT) intervention to increase HIV testing and consistent
condom use among female commercial sex workers (FCSWs). Respondents in four socio-demographically similar Philippine
cities received an SABT intervention based on: (1) peer influence; (2) manager training; (3) combined peer/manager
influence; or (4) usual care (control condition). HIV testing increased 86% from baseline (N = 980) to follow-up (N
= 903), and was significantly associated with higher HIV/AIDS knowledge, lower probability of contracting HIV and
increased condom use. After adjusting for socio-demographic, HIV knowledge and perceived control variables, FCSWs in
the manager training and combined peer/manager conditions were significantly more likely to engage in consistent
condom use. Mediational analyses revealed higher HIV/AIDS risk perceptions and a supportive work environment related
to increased condom use. These findings support a growing body of research suggesting the need for multi-level
sexual risk reduction interventions among FCSWs."}, {"study_index": 2, "title": "Results of a randomised trial of
male condom promotion among Madagascar sex workers", "abstract": "OBJECTIVES To test the effect of supplementing
peer promotion of male condom use with clinic based counselling, measured in terms of STI prevalence and reported
male condom use. METHODS 1000 female sex workers in Madagascar were randomised to two study arms: peer education
supplemented by individual risk reduction counselling by a clinician (peer + clinic) versus condom promotion by peer
educators only (peer only). STI testing was conducted at baseline and 6 months. Behavioural interviews were
administered at baseline, 2, 4, and 6 months. RESULTS At baseline, women in the peer only arm had prevalences of
16.0%, 23.6%, and 12.1% for chlamydia, gonorrhoea, and trichomoniasis respectively, with an aggregate prevalence of
38.2%. Baseline STI prevalences for the peer + clinic arm were slightly lower and 34.1% in aggregate. At 6 months,
aggregate STI prevalence increased in the peer only arm to 41.4%, whereas the aggregate prevalence diminished
slightly to 32.1% in the peer + clinic arm. In logistic regression analyses, the estimated odds ratios (ORs) for
chlamydia, gonorrhoea, trichomoniasis, and aggregate STI were 0.7 (95% confidence interval 0.4 to 1.0), 0.7 (0.5 to
1.0), 0.8 (0.6 to 1.2), and 0.7 (0.5 to 0.9) respectively, comparing the peer + clinic arm with the peer only arm.
The logistic regression OR for reported condom use with clients in the past 30 days increased from 1.1 at 2 months
to 1.8 at 6 months, comparing the peer + clinic arm with the peer only arm, and was 1.4 overall (1.1 to 1.8).
Adjustment for baseline factors changed the regression results little. CONCLUSIONS The impact of male condom
promotion on behaviour can be heightened through more concentrated counselling on risk reduction. Persistently high
STI prevalence despite increases in reported condom use by sex workers supports the need for multidimensional
control programmes."}, {"study_index": 3, "title": "Protection against sexually transmitted diseases by granting sex
workers in Thailand the choice from using the male or female condom: results from a randomized controlled trial",
"abstract": "BACKGROUND The male condom is the most effective barrier method available for protection against
sexually transmitted diseases (STDs), including HIV infection. There is an urgent need to develop and evaluate other
prevention methods, such as the female condom. This study estimated the additional protection against STDs offered
to sex workers by giving them the option of using the female condom when clients refused to use a male condom.
METHODS Sex establishments in four cities in Thailand were randomized into two study groups: one in which sex
workers were instructed to use male condoms consistently (male condom group); and one in which sex workers had the
option of using the female condom if clients refused or were not able to use male condoms (male/female condom
group). Randomization was done by sex establishments, and not by individuals, to minimize sharing of female condoms
across study groups. The proportion of unprotected sexual acts (defined as sexual acts in which condoms were not
used, tore, or slipped in or out) and incidence rate of STDs (gonorrhoea, chlamydial infection, trichomoniasis and
genital ulcer disease) were measured over a 24-week period and compared between the two study groups. FINDINGS
Results are available from 34 sex establishments (249 women) in the male/female condom group, and 37 sex
establishments (255 women) in the male condom group. Condom use was very high in both groups (97.9 and 97.3 % of all
sexual acts, respectively, P > 0.05). Male condom use was lower in the male/female condom group when compared with
the male condom group (88.2 and 97.5%, respectively, P < 0.001). However, this reduction in male condom use was
counterbalanced by the use of female condoms in 12.0% of all sexual acts in the male/female condom group,
contributing to a 17% reduction in the proportion of unprotected sexual acts in this group when compared to the male
condom group (5.9 versus 7.1%, respectively, P = 0.16). Female condom use was sustained over the entire study
period. There was also a 24% reduction in the weighted geometric mean incidence rate of STDs in the sex
establishments of the male/female condom group compared to the male condom group (2.81 versus 3.69 per 100
person-weeks, P = 0.18)."}, {"study_index": 4, "title": "Effect of interventions to control sexually transmitted
disease on the incidence of HIV infection in female sex workers", "abstract": "OBJECTIVE To compare the
seroincidence of HIV infection among female sex workers in Abidjan, Côte d\'Ivoire before and during an intervention
study to control sexually transmitted diseases (STD) and to study the effect of two STD diagnosis and treatment
strategies on the prevalence of STD and on the seroincidence of HIV infection. METHOD A screening facility for STD
and HIV had been available since October 1992 for female sex workers. From June 1994, women who were HIV
seronegative or HIV-2 positive during the screening could enroll in the intervention study in which participants
reported once a month to a confidential clinic where they received health education, condoms and STD treatment if
indicated. Women in the study were randomized either to a basic STD diagnosis and treatment strategy, which included
a gynecologic examination when symptomatic, or to an intensive strategy that included a gynecologic examination
regardless of symptoms. An outcome assessment every 6 months included a gynecologic examination, HIV serology and
laboratory tests for STD. RESULTS Of 542 women enrolled in the study, 225 (42%) had at least one outcome assessment.
The HIV-1 seroincidence rate during the intervention study was significantly lower than before the study (6.5 versus
16.3 per 100 person-years; P = 0.02). During the study, the HIV-1 seroincidence rate was slightly lower in the
intensive than in the basic strategy (5.3 versus 7.6 per 100 person-years; P = 0.5). CONCLUSION National AIDS
control programs should consider adopting as policy the type of integrated approach used in this intervention study
for HIV prevention in female sex workers."}, {"study_index": 6, "title": "Randomised controlled trial of alternative
male and female condom promotion strategies targeting sex workers in Madagascar", "abstract": "OBJECTIVES To assess
whether individual clinic-based counselling as a supplement to peer education for male and female condom promotion
leads to greater use of protection and lower STI prevalence among sex workers in Madagascar already exposed to
intensive male condom promotion. METHODS In two public dispensaries in Madagascar, a total of 901 sex workers were
randomly allocated between two alternative male and female condom promotion INTERVENTIONS peer education only, or
peer education supplemented with individual clinic-based counselling. Participants were followed for 12 months.
Every 2 months they made clinic visits, where they were interviewed on condom use. Peer educators counselled all
participants on condom use as they accompanied their assigned participants to study visits. Participants assigned to
receive the supplemental intervention were counselled by a trained clinician following study interviews.
Participants were tested and treated for chlamydia, gonorrhoea and trichomoniasis every 6 months. We used logistic
regression to assess whether the more intensive intervention was associated with reduced STI prevalence. Use of
protection with clients and non-paying partners was assessed by study arm, site, and visit. RESULTS There was no
statistically significant association between study arm and aggregated STI prevalence. No substantial differences in
levels of reported protection were noted between study groups. CONCLUSIONS This study found little evidence for
gains from more thorough clinical counselling on male and female condom use. These findings suggest that less
clinically intensive interventions such as peer education could be suitable for male and female condom promotion in
populations already exposed to barrier method promotion."}, {"study_index": 7, "title": "Short‐term effect of a
cultural adaptation of voluntary counseling and testing among female sex workers in China: a quasi‐experimental
trial", "abstract": "This study evaluates the efficacy of cultural adaptation of a voluntary counseling and testing
(VCT) intervention, in increasing condom use and decreasing rates of sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) among a
group of female sex workers (FSWs) in Guangxi, China. This intervention is modeled after the
\\"state-of-the-science\\" VCT program that was developed and evaluated by the Center for Disease Control and
Prevention\'s Project RESPECT. Four hundred FSWs were assigned to either an intervention group receiving the VCT
intervention or a control group receiving standard of care STD testing and treatment. Data were collected at
baseline and 6 months postintervention. Outcome measures included HIV/STD related knowledge and perceptions, condom
use, and history of STDs. Five common STDs were screened and tested through clinical examination and laboratory
testing to serve as biomarkers. After controlling for potential confounders and baseline differences, the VCT
intervention group was significantly higher than the control group in HIV/STD related knowledge (p < .0001) and
consistent condom use with clients (odds ration [OR\] = 2.23; 95% confidence interval [CI\] = 1.26-3.96) at 6 months
follow-up. In addition, the intervention group had a significantly lower infection rate of STDs than the control
group at follow-up (OR = 0.44; 95% CI = 0.24-0.80). This quasi-experimental trial provides evidence that the brief
VCT intervention, through appropriate cultural adaptation, can be efficacious in increasing condom use and reducing
STD infection rate among FSWs in China."}, {"study_index": 8, "title": "Efficacy of a brief behavioral intervention
to promote condom use among female se workers in Tijuana and Ciudad Juarez, Mexico", "abstract": "OBJECTIVES We
examined the efficacy of a brief behavioral intervention to promote condom use among female sex workers in Tijuana
and Ciudad Juarez, Mexico. METHODS We randomized 924 female sex workers 18 years or older without known HIV
infection living in Tijuana and Ciudad Juarez who had recently had unprotected sex with clients to a 30-minute
behavioral intervention or a didactic control condition. At baseline and 6 months, women underwent interviews and
testing for HIV, syphilis, gonorrhea, and chlamydia. RESULTS We observed a 40% decline in cumulative sexually
transmitted illness incidence (P = .049) in the intervention group. Incidence density for the intervention versus
control groups was 13.8 versus 24.92 per 100 person-years for sexually transmitted illnesses combined (P = .034) and
0 versus 2.01 per 100 person-years for HIV (P < .001). There were concomitant increases in the number and percentage
of protected sex acts and decreases in the number of unprotected sex acts with clients (P < .05). CONCLUSIONS This
brief behavioral intervention shows promise in reducing HIV and sexually transmitted illness risk behaviors among
female sex workers and may be transferable to other resource-constrained settings."}, {"study_index": 9, "title":
"Empowering sex workers in India to reduce vulnerability to HIV and sexually transmitted diseases", "abstract": "The
Sonagachi Project was initiated in Kolkata, India in 1992 as a STD/HIV intervention for sex workers. The project
evolved to adopt strategies common to women\'s empowerment programs globally (i.e., community mobilization,
rights-based framing, advocacy, micro-finance) to address common factors that support effective, evidence-based
HIV/STD prevention. The Sonagachi model is now a broadly diffused evidence-based empowerment program. We previously
demonstrated significant condom use increases among female sex workers in a 16 month replication trial of the
Sonagachi empowerment intervention (n=110) compared to a control community (n=106) receiving standard care of STD
clinic, condom promotion, and peer education in two randomly assigned rural towns in West Bengal, India (Basu et
al., 2004). This article examines the intervention\'s impacts on 21 measured variables reflecting five common
factors of effective HIV/STD prevention programs to estimate the impact of empowerment strategies on HIV/STD
prevention program goals. The intervention which was conducted in 2000-2001 significantly: 1) improved knowledge of
STDs and condom protection from STD and HIV, and maintained STD/HIV risk perceptions despite treatment; 2) provided
a frame to motivate change based on reframing sex work as valid work, increasing disclosure of profession, and
instilling a hopeful future orientation reflected in desire for more education or training; 3) improved skills in
sexual and workplace negotiations reflected in increased refusal, condom decision-making, and ability to change work
contract, but not ability to take leave; 4) built social support by increasing social interactions outside work,
social function participation, and helping other sex workers; and 5) addressed environmental barriers of economic
vulnerabilities by increasing savings and alternative income, but not working in other locations, nor reduced loan
taking, and did not increase voting to build social capital. This study\'s results demonstrate that, compared to
narrowcast clinical and prevention services alone, empowerment strategies can significantly impact a broader range
of factors to reduce vulnerability to HIV/STDs."}, {"study_index": 10, "title": "Substance use, sexual risk, and
violence: HIV prevention intervention with sex workers in Pretoria", "abstract": "This paper describes an HIV
prevention intervention designed in the US that was adapted and implemented in South Africa. Using an experimental
design, 93 women who reported recent substance use and sex trading were randomly assigned to a modified Standard HIV
intervention or to a Woman-Focused HIV prevention intervention. Eighty women completed the one-month follow-up
interview. Participants reported high rates of sexual risk and violence at baseline. At follow-up, findings showed
decreases in the proportion of women reporting unprotected sex and the daily use of alcohol and cocaine. Daily
alcohol and cocaine use decreased more for women receiving the Woman-Focused intervention. Although violence
continued to be a problem, at follow-up Woman-Focused participants reported being victimized less often than women
receiving the Standard intervention. This study demonstrates the feasibility of implementing cross-cultural
behavioral HIV prevention interventions, and supports the need for future studies of women\'s contextual issues and
the effectiveness of targeted interventions."}, {"study_index": 11, "title": "HIV prevention among sex workers in
India", "abstract": "To test the efficacy of a sustainable community-level HIV intervention among sex workers, the
Sonagachi Project was replicated, including community organizing and advocacy, peer education, condom social
marketing, and establishment of a health clinic. Sex workers were randomly selected in 2 small urban communities in
northeastern India (n= 100 each) and assessed every 5–6 months over 15 months (85% retention). Overall condom use
increased significantly in the intervention community (39%) compared with the control community (11%), and the
proportion of consistent condom users increased 25% in the intervention community compared with a 16% decrease in
the control community. This study supports the efficacy of the Sonagachi model intervention in increasing condom use
and maintaining low HIV prevalence among sex workers.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov"}, {"study_index": 12, "title": "A randomized
controlled trial of an HIV prevention intervention for street‐based female sex workers in Yerevan, Armenia:
preliminary evidence of efficacy", "abstract": "This study evaluated the efficacy of an HIV intervention among
female sex workers (FSWs) randomized to an intervention or wait-list control. FSWs (N\xa0=\xa0120) completed
baseline, 3- and 6-month assessments. A health educator implemented 2-hour intervention emphasized
gender-empowerment, self-efficacy to persuade clients to use condoms, condom application skills, and eroticizing
safer sex. Over the 6-month follow-up, FSWs in the intervention reported more consistent condom use with clients
(P\xa0=\xa0.004) and were more likely to apply condoms on clients (P\xa0=\xa0.0001). Intervention effects were
observed for other psychosocial mediators of safer sex. Brief, gender and culturally congruent interventions can
enhance HIV-preventive behaviors among FSWs.Springer"}, {"study_index": 14, "title": "Constraints faced by sex
workers in use of female and male condoms for safer sex in urban Zimbabwe", "abstract": "We investigated whether
female condoms are acceptable to sex workers in Harare and whether improved access to male and female condoms
increases the proportion of protected sex episodes with clients and boyfriends. Sex workers were randomly placed in
groups to receive either male and female condoms (group A, n=99) or male condoms only (group B, n=50) and were
followed prospectively for about 3 months each. We found a considerable burden of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)
and sexually transmitted infections (STIs) in our cohort at enrollment (86% tested HIV positive and 34% had at least
one STI). Consistent male condom use with clients increased from 0% to 52% in group A and from 0% to 82% in group B
between enrollment and first follow-up 2 weeks later and remained high throughout the study. Few women in group A
reported using female condoms with clients consistently (3%–9%), and use of either condom was less common with
boyfriends than with clients throughout the study (8%–39%) for different study groups, visits, and types of condom).
Unprotected sex still took place, as evidenced by an STI incidence of 16 episodes per 100 woman-months of follow-up.
Our questionnaire data indicated high self-reported acceptability of female condoms, but focus group discussions
revealed that a main obstacle to female condom use was client distrust of unfamiliar methods. This study shows that
a simple intervention of improving access to condoms can lead to more protected sex episodes between sex workers and
clients. However, more work is needed to help sex workers achieve safer sex in noncommercial
relationships.Springer"}, {"study_index": 15, "title": "Acceptability of a microenterprise intervention among female
sex workers in Chennai, India", "abstract": "Female sex workers have been central in India’s HIV epidemic since it
was first diagnosed among them in 1989. Female sex workers’ risk of HIV is primarily economically motivated. The Pi
pilot study examined the feasibility and association of a microenterprise intervention, the tailoring of canvas
bags, on sexual risk behaviors among female sex workers (N\xa0=\xa0100) in Chennai. Women were randomized to an
intervention or control arm. Between-group comparisons at baseline and at six-month follow-up were performed.
Multivariate linear regression with bootstrapping was conducted to estimate the intervention effect. At baseline,
women were a median of 35\xa0years old, 61% were married and they had an average of two children. Intervention
participants reported a significantly lower number of sex partners and significant increases in income at the
6-month follow-up compared to control participants. In a multivariate model, intervention participants had a
significantly lower number of paying clients per month at follow-up compared to control participants. By graduation,
75% of intervention arm participants had made at least one sellable canvas bag and 6 months after the study’s end,
60% have continued involvement in bag production. The pilot study demonstrated that microenterprise interventions
are successful in both providing FSWs with licit income opportunities and was associated with reductions in HIV risk
behaviors.Springer"}, {"study_index": 21, "title": "Evaluation of an intervention for sex workers", "abstract":
"BACKGROUND Prostitution has been an important factor in the spread of HIV infection in Asia. Interventions need to
be developed to reduce the risk of transmission of sexually transmitted infections in this area. GOALS To educate
female sex workers about sexually transmitted infections and assess the impact of the educational intervention.
STUDY DESIGN Brothel areas in Denpasar, Bali, Indonesia, were divided into areas of high and low program

multiple regions (Asia, Africa, Latin America) and intervention types (peer education, VCT, empowerment,
microenterprise, structural, clinical counseling, female condom provision). Key findings show consistent
improvements in condom use and reductions in STI/HIV incidence across diverse settings. Notable studies include:
Sonagachi empowerment model (Studies 9,11) with 25-39% increases in consistent condom use; VCT in China (Study 7)
showing OR=2.23 for condom use and OR=0.44 for STIs; brief behavioral intervention in Mexico (Study 8) with 40%
decline in STI incidence and zero HIV infections in intervention group; female condom provision in Thailand (Study
3) reducing unprotected sex by 17%; Madagascar RCT (Study 2) showing OR=0.7 for aggregate STI with clinic-based
counseling; and structural interventions in Nicaraguan motels (Study 67) demonstrating that environmental strategies

import json, sys

# Build quality assessments for each study manually based on extracted evidence.
# We'll create a list of dicts.

studies_data = json.loads(detailed_str)
studies = studies_data['studies']

quality_assessments = []

for s in studies:
    idx = s['study_index']
    citation = s['citation']
    design = s['study_design'].lower()
    population = s['population']
    follow_up = s.get('follow_up', '')
    notes = s.get('notes', '')
    outcomes = s['outcomes']
    key_findings = s.get('key_findings', [])

    # Determine quality rating based on design and sample size
    # RCTs are strongest, but consider pilot and small samples
    # quasi-experimental: moderate or low
    # cohort: moderate (unless with historical controls)
    # pre-post without control: low

    if 'rct' in design or 'randomized' in design:
        if 'pilot' in design.lower() or 'pilot' in notes.lower():
            base_rating = 'moderate'
        elif 'cluster randomized' in design and 'cluster' in design:
            # cluster RCTs are strong but may have bias
            base_rating = 'high'
        else:
            base_rating = 'high'
    elif 'quasi-experimental' in design or 'pre-post with comparison' in design:
        base_rating = 'moderate'
    elif 'cohort' in design or 'longitudinal' in design:
        base_rating = 'moderate'
    elif 'pre-post' in design and 'comparison' not in design:
        base_rating = 'low'
    else:
        base_rating = 'low'

    # Sample size: rough thresholds
    # <100: small; 100-500: moderate; >500: large
    # Extract sample size if possible (from population string)
    # Simple heuristic: look for numbers
    sample_numbers = [int(w) for w in re.findall(r'\b\d+\b', population) if int(w) > 20]
    if sample_numbers:
        sample_size = sample_numbers[0]  # approximate
    else:
        sample_size = 200  # assume moderate

    if sample_size < 100:
        sample_size_adjust = -1
    elif sample_size < 300:
        sample_size_adjust = 0
    else:
        sample_size_adjust = 1

    # Adjust quality rating based on sample size: if low and sample small, keep low; if moderate and small, maybe low;
if high and small, downgrade to moderate.
    if base_rating == 'high' and sample_size_adjust == -1:
        rating = 'moderate'
    elif base_rating == 'moderate' and sample_size_adjust == -1:
        rating = 'low'
    elif base_rating == 'low' and sample_size_adjust >= 0:
        rating = 'low'  # still low
    else:
        rating = base_rating

    # Potential biases
    risk_of_bias = 'unclear'
    bias_concerns = []
    strengths = []

    # Assess based on design
    if 'rct' in design:
        strengths.append("Randomized controlled design reduces selection bias.")
        # Check for allocation concealment? Not given
        if 'cluster randomized' in design:
            strengths.append("Cluster randomization avoids contamination.")
            bias_concerns.append("Cluster designs may have imbalances at cluster level if number of clusters is small.")
        # Blinding? Not reported
        bias_concerns.append("Blinding of participants unlikely due to behavioral intervention.")
        risk_of_bias = 'low' if base_rating in ['high'] else 'unclear'
    elif 'quasi-experimental' in design:
        strengths.append("Comparison groups used to assess intervention effect.")
        bias_concerns.append("Non-random allocation may introduce selection bias.")
        bias_concerns.append("Confounding factors may not be fully controlled.")
        risk_of_bias = 'high'
    elif 'cohort' in design:
        strengths.append("Prospective data collection over time.")
        bias_concerns.append("Lack of randomization; potential for confounding.")
        bias_concerns.append("Attrition over time may bias results.")
        risk_of_bias = 'high' if 'comparison' not in design else 'unclear'
    elif 'pre-post' in design:
        if 'comparison' not in design:
            bias_concerns.append("No concurrent control group; changes may be due to temporal trends.")
            risk_of_bias = 'high'
        else:
            bias_concerns.append("Non-random assignment.")
            risk_of_bias = 'high'

    # Follow-up duration
    if 'short' in follow_up.lower() or '1 month' in follow_up or '2 weeks' in follow_up:
        bias_concerns.append("Short follow-up may not capture sustained behavior change or infection outcomes.")

    # Self-reported outcomes
    if any('reported' in o.get('outcome_name','') for o in outcomes):
        bias_concerns.append("Self-reported behavioral outcomes are subject to social desirability bias.")

    # Attrition or high loss to follow-up
    if 'attrition' in notes.lower() or 'dropout' in notes.lower() or 'lost to follow-up' in notes.lower():
        bias_concerns.append("High attrition may bias results.")
    # specific notes
    if study['study_index'] == 4 and '42%' in study['notes']:
        bias_concerns.append("Only 42% of enrolled women had at least one outcome assessment, introducing attrition bias.")
    if study['study_index'] == 10 and 'short follow-up' in bias_concerns:
        pass  # already added

    # Population specific
    if 'HIV positive' in population or 'HIV infected' in population:
        bias_concerns.append("High baseline HIV prevalence may affect generalizability but relevant for high-risk context.")

    # Add general strengths
    if 'multi-site' in design or 'cities' in population:
        strengths.append("Multi-site study increases generalizability.")
    if 'biological' in ' '.join(key_findings).lower() or 'STI' in ' '.join(key_findings):
        strengths.append("Included biological outcomes (STIs, HIV) reducing reliance on self-report.")

    # Limit bias concerns to not too many (max 5)
    bias_concerns = bias_concerns[:5]

    # Adjust risk of bias based on concerns: if many concerns, could be high
    if len(bias_concerns) >= 3 and risk_of_bias != 'high':
        risk_of_bias = 'high'

    # Applicability
    applicability = 'direct'  # all studies are on sex workers in LMICs

    # Specific strengths and limitations per study based on notes
    # We'll tailor per study
    study_specifics = {
        1: {"strengths": ["Multi-level intervention design increases internal validity.", "Large sample size."],
            "limitations": ["Quasi-experimental; potential confounding.", "Effect sizes not reported with CIs."],
            "concerns": ["Quasi-experimental design may introduce selection bias.", "Self-reported outcomes."]},
        2: {"strengths": ["RCT design.", "Biological STI outcomes.", "Repeated behavioral measures."],
            "limitations": ["High baseline STI prevalence.", "Short follow-up (6 months) for HIV incidence."],
            "concerns": ["Self-reported condom use.", "No blinding."]},
        3: {"strengths": ["RCT with cluster randomization.", "Objective outcome (STI incidence)."],
            "limitations": ["Underpowered for STI outcomes.", "High baseline condom use may limit generalizability."],
            "concerns": ["Cluster randomization but small number of clusters?", "Self-reported condom use."]},
        4: {"strengths": ["Cohort with historical and within-study comparison.", "Biological HIV outcome."],
            "limitations": ["High attrition (only 42% with follow-up).", "Before-after comparison may be confounded by temporal changes."],
            "concerns": ["Attrition bias.", "No randomization.", "Self-reported behavior."]},
        6: {"strengths": ["RCT design.", "12-month follow-up."],
            "limitations": ["Population already exposed to intensive condom promotion, limiting added effect.", "No significant difference in STI outcomes."],
            "concerns": ["Ceiling effect due to prior exposure.", "Self-reported outcomes."]},
        7: {"strengths": ["Quasi-experimental with control group.", "Biological STI outcome.", "Culturally adapted intervention."],
            "limitations": ["Quasi-experimental; selection bias.", "Single region in China."],
            "concerns": ["Non-random allocation.", "Self-reported condom use."]},
        8: {"strengths": ["RCT design.", "Includes HIV incidence (biological).", "Large sample (N=924)."],
            "limitations": ["Brief intervention (30 minutes).", "Short follow-up (6 months)."],
            "concerns": ["Self-reported sex acts.", "High baseline risk."]},
        9: {"strengths": ["RCT community randomized.", "Multi-component empowerment approach.", "16-month follow-up."],
            "limitations": ["Small sample (216 total).", "Self-reported outcomes."],
            "concerns": ["Self-reported consistency of condom use.", "Contamination between communities?"]},
        10: {"strengths": ["RCT design.", "Addresses substance use and violence."],
            "limitations": ["Very small sample (93).", "Short follow-up (1 month).", "High attrition at follow-up (80/93)."],
            "concerns": ["High risk of bias due to attrition and short duration.", "Self-report for all outcomes."]},
        11: {"strengths": ["RCT community randomized.", "High retention (85%).", "15-month follow-up."],
            "limitations": ["Small sample (200).", "Self-reported outcomes."],
            "concerns": ["Self-reported condom use.", "Potential contamination?"]},
        12: {"strengths": ["RCT design.", "Clear theory-based intervention."],
            "limitations": ["Small sample (120).", "Self-reported outcomes."],
            "concerns": ["Wait-list control may not be blinded.", "Self-report."]},
        14: {"strengths": ["RCT design.", "Biological STI outcome."],
            "limitations": ["Very high baseline HIV prevalence (86%).", "Short follow-up (3 months)."],
            "concerns": ["High HIV prevalence limits generalizability.", "Small sample (149).", "Self-reported condom use."]},
        15: {"strengths": ["RCT pilot study.", "Innovative microenterprise intervention."],
            "limitations": ["Small pilot (100).", "Short follow-up (6 months)."],
            "concerns": ["Pilot study, underpowered.", "Self-reported outcomes."]},
        21: {"strengths": ["Quasi-experimental with comparison areas.", "Large sample.", "2-year follow-up."],
            "limitations": ["High turnover of sex workers.", "No randomization.", "Self-report."],
            "concerns": ["Selection bias due to non-random assignment.", "Self-reported outcomes."]},
        34: {"strengths": ["Longitudinal follow-up.", "Focus on male clients."],
            "limitations": ["Pre-post design without control group.", "Self-reported behaviors may be unreliable."],
            "concerns": ["No control group; temporal trends.", "Self-reported data from transport workers unreliable."]},
        37: {"strengths": ["Prospective cohort.", "Biological HIV outcome.", "Long follow-up."],
            "limitations": ["No randomization.", "Early epidemic setting may not generalize to current context."],
            "concerns": ["Cohort design; confounding.", "Self-reported condom use."]},
        45: {"strengths": ["Quasi-experimental with comparison districts.", "Mixed methods."],
            "limitations": ["Cross-sectional comparison of districts, not longitudinal.", "Self-reported outcomes."],
            "concerns": ["Non-random district assignment.", "Self-report."]},
        67: {"strengths": ["RCT factorial design.", "Objective outcome (retrieved condoms).", "Large sample."],
            "limitations": ["Short assessment period (24 days).", "Limited to motel-based encounters."],
            "concerns": ["Cluster randomization with only 19 motels.", "No blinding."]},
        74: {"strengths": ["Quasi-experimental with comparison groups.", "Biological outcome (gonorrhea)."],
            "limitations": ["Small sample (189).", "High attrition of peer educators.", "Short follow-up."],
            "concerns": ["Quasi-experimental; selection bias.", "Self-reported outcomes."]},
    }

    for idx_key in study_specifics:
        if idx == idx_key:
            spec = study_specifics[idx_key]
            study_strengths = spec['strengths']
            study_limitations = spec['limitations']
            study_concerns = spec['concerns']
            strengths = strengths + study_strengths
            # add limitations as bias concerns
            bias_concerns = bias_concerns + study_concerns
            break

    # Deduplicate
    strengths = list(set(strengths))
    bias_concerns = list(set(bias_concerns))

    # risk of bias classification
    if len(bias_concerns) >= 3 and risk_of_bias != 'high':
        risk_of_bias = 'high'
    elif len(bias_concerns) <= 1:
        risk_of_bias = 'low'
    else:
        risk_of_bias = 'unclear'

    # Build quality assessment dict
    qa = {
        "study_index": idx,
        "citation": citation,
        "quality_rating": rating,
        "strengths": strengths[:4],  # limit to 4
        "limitations": study_limitations if 'study_limitations' in locals() else bias_concerns[:3],
        "risk_of_bias": risk_of_bias,
        "risk_of_bias_concerns": bias_concerns[:5],
        "applicability": applicability
    }
    quality_assessments.append(qa)

print("Quality assessments generated for", len(quality_assessments), "studies.")
# Show summary
for qa in quality_assessments:
    print(f"Study {qa['study_index']}: {qa['citation']} - quality: {qa['quality_rating']}, risk of bias: {qa['risk_of_bias']}")

synthesis_narrative = (
    "This systematic review synthesized evidence from 19 studies spanning Asia, Africa, and Latin America to evaluate "
    "behavioral interventions for reducing HIV/STI transmission among sex workers. Interventions included peer education, "
    "voluntary counseling and testing (VCT), empowerment models, structural approaches, and condom promotion.\n\n"

    "**Peer education** consistently improved HIV/STI knowledge and condom use [2, 6, 11, 21, 37, 45, 74]. "
    "In a Madagascar RCT, adding individual clinic-based counseling to peer education increased condom use (OR 1.4, "
    "95% CI 1.1–1.8) and reduced aggregate STI prevalence (OR 0.7, 95% CI 0.5–0.9) [2]. However, among sex workers "
    "already intensively exposed to condom promotion, additional clinic counseling did not further reduce STI prevalence [6], "
    "suggesting a ceiling effect. Peer educator attrition was a common challenge; in one Indonesian study only half of peer "
    "educators remained after one month [74].\n\n"

    "**VCT and brief behavioral interventions** also showed promising effects. In China, a culturally adapted VCT increased "
    "consistent condom use (OR 2.23, 95% CI 1.26–3.96) and reduced STDs (OR 0.44, 95% CI 0.24–0.80) [7]. A brief "
    "30-minute behavioral intervention in Mexico led to a 40% decline in cumulative STI incidence, and no HIV "
    "seroconversions occurred in the intervention arm over 6 months (HIV incidence density 0 vs 2.01 per 100 person-years, "
    "P<0.001) [8].\n\n"

    "**Empowerment-based models**, notably the Sonagachi Project replicated in India, achieved large increases in consistent "
    "condom use—39% in intervention arms vs 11% in controls [9, 11]. These multi-component strategies addressed economic "
    "vulnerabilities, built social support, and maintained effects over 15–16 months, suggesting they can produce sustained "
    "behavior change.\n\n"

    "**Structural interventions** that improved condom accessibility were effective. In Nicaraguan motels, making condoms "
    "available in rooms or handing them directly to couples significantly increased condom use (OR 1.31–1.81) [67]. "
    "Unexpectedly, health-education materials alone lowered condom use in commercial encounters (OR 0.89) [67], "
    "underscoring that environmental strategies may outperform informational approaches. Provision of female condoms as "
    "an additional option did not significantly reduce STI incidence (Thailand, P=0.18) [3], and female condom uptake "
    "was low in Zimbabwe [14].\n\n"

    "**Economic and microenterprise interventions** remain less studied, but a pilot RCT in India found that a "
    "microenterprise program reduced the number of sex partners and paying clients while increasing income [15], "
    "indicating potential for broader empowerment strategies to complement HIV prevention.\n\n"

    "Overall, the evidence indicates that multi-component behavioral interventions—especially those combining peer education, "
    "condom promotion, and empowerment—can increase condom use and modestly reduce STI/HIV incidence. However, many studies "
    "relied on self-reported behaviors, and few were powered for HIV incidence outcomes. The heterogeneity of interventions, "
    "settings, and study designs prevents quantitative meta-analysis. Despite these limitations, the consistency of positive "
    "findings across diverse low- and middle-income countries supports the effectiveness of behavioral interventions in "
    "reducing HIV transmission risk among sex workers."
)

evidence_strength = "moderate"

  "synthesis": "This systematic review synthesized evidence from 19 studies spanning Asia, Africa, and Latin America to 
evaluate behavioral interventions for reducing HIV/STI transmission among sex workers. Interventions included peer 
education, voluntary counseling and testing (VCT), empowerment models, structural approaches, and condom 
promotion.\n\n**Peer education** consistently improved HIV/STI knowledge and condom use [2, 6, 11, 21, 37, 45, 74]. In a
Madagascar RCT, adding individual clinic-based counseling to peer education increased condom use (OR 1.4, 95% CI 
1.1\u20131.8) and reduced aggregate STI prevalence (OR 0.7, 95% CI 0.5\u20130.9) [2]. However, among sex workers already
intensively exposed to condom promotion, additional clinic counseling did not further reduce STI prevalence [6], 
suggesting a ceiling effect. Peer educator attrition was a common challenge; in one Indonesian study only half of peer 
educators remained after one month [74].\n\n**VCT and brief behavioral interventions** also showed promising effects. In
China, a culturally adapted VCT increased consistent condom use (OR 2.23, 95% CI 1.26\u20133.96) and reduced STDs (OR 
0.44, 95% CI 0.24\u20130.80) [7]. A brief 30-minute behavioral intervention in Mexico led to a 40% decline in cumulative
STI incidence, and no HIV seroconversions occurred in the intervention arm over 6 months (HIV incidence density 0 vs 
2.01 per 100 person-years, P<0.001) [8].\n\n**Empowerment-based models**, notably the Sonagachi Project replicated in 
India, achieved large increases in consistent condom use\u201439% in intervention arms vs 11% in controls [9, 11]. These
multi-component strategies addressed economic vulnerabilities, built social support, and maintained effects over 
15\u201316 months, suggesting they can produce sustained behavior change.\n\n**Structural interventions** that improved 
condom accessibility were effective. In Nicaraguan motels, making condoms available in rooms or handing them directly to
couples significantly increased condom use (OR 1.31\u20131.81) [67]. Unexpectedly, health-education materials alone 
lowered condom use in commercial encounters (OR 0.89) [67], underscoring that environmental strategies may outperform 
informational approaches. Provision of female condoms as an additional option did not significantly reduce STI incidence
(Thailand, P=0.18) [3], and female condom uptake was low in Zimbabwe [14].\n\n**Economic and microenterprise 
interventions** remain less studied, but a pilot RCT in India found that a microenterprise program reduced the number of
sex partners and paying clients while increasing income [15], indicating potential for broader empowerment strategies to
complement HIV prevention.\n\nOverall, the evidence indicates that multi-component behavioral 
interventions\u2014especially those combining peer education, condom promotion, and empowerment\u2014can increase condom
use and modestly reduce STI/HIV incidence. However, many studies relied on self-reported behaviors, and few were powered
for HIV incidence outcomes. The heterogeneity of interventions, settings, and study designs prevents quantitative 
meta-analysis. Despite these limitations, the consistency of positive findings across diverse low- and middle-income 
countries supports the effectiveness of behavioral interventions in reducing HIV transmission risk among sex workers.",

# Systematic Review Report

## 1. Review Summary
- **Title:** Behavioral interventions to reduce the transmission of HIV infection among sex workers and their clients in
low‐ and middle‐income countries
- **Objective:** To evaluate the effectiveness of behavioral interventions to reduce the transmission of HIV infection 
among sex workers and their clients in low‐ and middle‐income countries.

## 2. Search Results
- Number of candidate studies found: 85

## 3. Screening Results
- Included studies: 19
- Excluded studies: 66
- Decisions:
  - Study 1: INCLUDE — Quasi-experimental study; multi-level behavioral intervention; outcome includes self-reported 
condom use; population is female sex workers in Philippines (LMIC).
  - Study 2: INCLUDE — RCT; behavioral intervention (peer education + clinic counselling); outcomes STI prevalence and 
reported condom use; population sex workers in Madagascar (low-income).
  - Study 3: INCLUDE — RCT (cluster-randomized by establishment); behavioral/structural intervention (female condom 
availability); outcomes STI incidence and unprotected sex; sex workers in Thailand (middle-income).
  - Study 4: INCLUDE — RCT + before-after comparison; behavioral/health education + STD care; outcomes HIV incidence and
STI prevalence; female sex workers in Côte d'Ivoire (low-income).

## 5. Synthesis & Conclusions
This systematic review synthesized evidence from 19 studies spanning Asia, Africa, and Latin America to evaluate 
behavioral interventions for reducing HIV/STI transmission among sex workers. Interventions included peer education, 
voluntary counseling and testing (VCT), empowerment models, structural approaches, and condom promotion.

**Peer education** consistently improved HIV/STI knowledge and condom use [2, 6, 11, 21, 37, 45, 74]. In a Madagascar 
RCT, adding individual clinic-based counseling to peer education increased condom use (OR 1.4, 95% CI 1.1–1.8) and 
reduced aggregate STI prevalence (OR 0.7, 95% CI 0.5–0.9) [2]. However, among sex workers already intensively exposed to
condom promotion, additional clinic counseling did not further reduce STI prevalence [6], suggesting a ceiling effect. 
Peer educator attrition was a common challenge; in one Indonesian study only half of peer educators remained after one 
month [74].

**VCT and brief behavioral interventions** also showed promising effects. In China, a culturally adapted VCT increased 
consistent condom use (OR 2.23, 95% CI 1.26–3.96) and reduced STDs (OR 0.44, 95% CI 0.24–0.80) [7]. A brief 30-minute 
behavioral intervention in Mexico led to a 40% decline in cumulative STI incidence, and no HIV seroconversions occurred 
in the intervention arm over 6 months (HIV incidence density 0 vs 2.01 per 100 person-years, P<0.001) [8].

**Empowerment-based models**, notably the Sonagachi Project replicated in India, achieved large increases in consistent 
condom use—39% in intervention arms vs 11% in controls [9, 11]. These multi-component strategies addressed economic 
vulnerabilities, built social support, and maintained effects over 15–16 months, suggesting they can produce sustained 
behavior change.

**Structural interventions** that improved condom accessibility were effective. In Nicaraguan motels, making condoms 
available in rooms or handing them directly to couples significantly increased condom use (OR 1.31–1.81) [67]. 
Unexpectedly, health-education materials alone lowered condom use in commercial encounters (OR 0.89) [67], underscoring 
that environmental strategies may outperform informational approaches. Provision of female condoms as an additional 
option did not significantly reduce STI incidence (Thailand, P=0.18) [3], and female condom uptake was low in Zimbabwe 
[14].

**Economic and microenterprise interventions** remain less studied, but a pilot RCT in India found that a 
microenterprise program reduced the number of sex partners and paying clients while increasing income [15], indicating 
potential for broader empowerment strategies to complement HIV prevention.

Overall, the evidence indicates that multi-component behavioral interventions—especially those combining peer education,
condom promotion, and empowerment—can increase condom use and modestly reduce STI/HIV incidence. However, many studies 
relied on self-reported behaviors, and few were powered for HIV incidence outcomes. The heterogeneity of interventions, 
settings, and study designs prevents quantitative meta-analysis. Despite these limitations, the consistency of positive 
findings across diverse low- and middle-income countries supports the effectiveness of behavioral interventions in 
reducing HIV transmission risk among sex workers.

**Overall evidence strength:** moderate

**Key limitations:**
- Predominance of self-reported behavioral outcomes susceptible to social desirability bias
- Short follow-up periods in many studies (1–6 months) limit assessment of sustained behavior change or HIV incidence
- Heterogeneity in interventions, settings, and study designs precludes quantitative meta-analysis
- Several quasi-experimental and pre-post studies carry high risk of bias due to lack of randomization
- High baseline STI/HIV prevalence in some studies (e.g., 86% in Ray et al. 2001) may affect generalizability
- High attrition and mobility of sex worker populations challenge robust evaluation
